translations.text: Jesus went into a city that is called Nain, and so on.
Our Lord went to a certain city called Nain, together with his disciples and a great crowd. When he came near the town gate, a young man's body was being carried out for burial, and so on.
Bede the commentator said that the city of Nain is interpreted as 'wave' or 'commotion.'
The dead young man, who was carried out in the sight of many people, signifies every sinful person who is killed in the inner man by grave sins, and whose wickedness is known to people.

The young man was the only son of his mother. In the same way every Christian is spiritually a son of the holy Church, which is the mother of us all and yet an undefiled virgin, because her offspring is not bodily but spiritual.
Every servant of God, when he is learning, is called a child; and when he teaches another, he is a mother. As the apostle Paul said about those who had fallen away,
"You are my children, whom I now conceive a second time, until Christ is renewed in you." The town gate signifies a bodily sense through which people sin.
The man who sows discord among Christians, or who speaks iniquity on high through the gate of his mouth, is carried out dead.
He who looks at a woman with a lecherous gaze and foul lust, through the gate of his eyes, shows that his soul is dead.
Whoever gladly listens to idle talk or slanderous words makes his ear a gate of death for himself. The same is to be understood of the other senses.
The Saviour was moved with compassion for the mother, to give us an example of his kindness; and afterwards he raised the dead man, to strengthen us in faith in him.
He came near and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. The bier that carried the dead man is the untroubled conscience of the sinner who has no hope.
Truly, the bearers who carried him to burial are the flatteries of fawning companions, who with flattery and poisoned sweet words urge on and praise the sinner, just as the prophet said:
"The sinner is praised in his desires, and the unrighteous man is blessed." When he is surrounded by empty fame and flattery, it is as if he were buried under a heap of earth.
About such people the Saviour spoke to one of his chosen followers, when that man wanted to bury his father's body. He said, "Let the dead bury their dead; you go and proclaim the kingdom of God."
Truly, the dead bury other dead when sinful people flatter others like themselves with harmful praise and crush them under the piled-up weight of the worst flattery.
About such people it is said in another place, "The tongues of flatterers bind people's souls in sins."
When the Lord touched the bier, the bearers stood still. In the same way, if the sinner's conscience is touched with fear of the judgment on high,
then he resists sinful desires and lying flatterers, and promptly answers the Lord who calls him to eternal life, as if he rose from death.
The Lord said to the young man, "I say to you, arise." And he immediately sat up and spoke, and the Saviour gave him to his mother.
The revived man sits up when the sinner comes back to life through divine compunction. He speaks when he occupies his mouth with praises of God and seeks God's mercy through true confession.
He is handed over to his mother when, through the authority of priests, he is joined to the fellowship of the holy Church. The people were struck with great fear;
For just as a person turns from greater sins to God's mercy and corrects his conduct according to God's commandments, so more people are turned to the praise of God through his example.
The people said that a great prophet had arisen among us, and that God had visited his people. They spoke truly of Christ, that he is a great prophet;
but he is the Prophet of prophets, and the prophecy of them all; for they all prophesied about him, and by his coming he fulfilled the prophecy of them all.
We now say with greater faith that he is a great prophet, because he knows all things, and he also prophesied much, and he is true God of true God,
the Almighty Son of the Almighty Father, who visited his people through his human nature and set them free from slavery to the devil.
We read in many places in books that the Saviour raised many dead people to life, but no gospel account is given of any of them except three only.
One is this young man of whom we have just spoken. The second was the daughter of a ruler. The third was Lazarus, the brother of Martha and Mary.
The rising of these three people signifies the threefold rising of sinful souls.
The death of the soul is of three kinds: the first is evil consent, the second is evil deed, and the third is evil habit.
The ruler's daughter lay at the point of death, and the father invited the Saviour to come there, because at that time he was nearby.
She died before he reached her. When he came, he took her by the hand and said,
"Maiden, I say to you, arise." And she arose at once and asked for food.
This maiden, who lay inside, put to sleep in death, signifies the death of the sinful soul that secretly delights in evil desires, while it is not yet known to men that it is dead through sins;

but Christ showed that he would bring such a sinful soul to life, if he is called to it with earnest prayers, when he raised the maiden inside the house, just as a secret sin lies hidden in the human heart.

Now there are other sinners who delight in harmful desires with consent, and also make their wickedness known by deeds; such were signified by the dead young man who was carried in the sight of the people.
Christ raises such sinners if they repent of their sins, and he hands them over to their mother; that is, he joins them to the unity of his Church.
Some sinful men consent to their desires, and through evil deeds make their sins known to men, and also defile themselves by sinning habitually:
such were signified by Lazarus, who lay in the tomb four nights, stinking foully. Truly God's name is Almighty, because he can accomplish all things.

He can bring the sinful soul to life through his grace, even though it stinks foully in habitual sins, if it seeks God's mercy with careful conduct of life; but the greater the wound, the greater the remedy it needs.
The Saviour showed this when he raised the girl with a gentle voice in the sight of a few people;
because he did not allow any more people to be inside except the father and the mother and his three disciples; and then he said, "Maiden, arise."
So also the hidden death of the soul that sins secretly by consent is more easily raised than open sins are healed.
he raised the young man in the sight of all the people and strengthened him with these words: "Young man, I say to you, arise."
Secret sins must be atoned for secretly, and open ones openly, so that those who were previously led astray by a person's wicked deeds may be built up by his repentance.
When the Lord raised Lazarus, who was already stinking, he was troubled in himself, shed tears, and called out with a loud voice,

"Lazarus, come forth." By this he showed that whoever has sinned for a very long time and out of habit must also, with great repentance and weeping, draw himself away from his evil habits to God's righteousness.
No sin is so great that a person cannot atone for it, if with an inward heart he perseveres in true penance in proportion to the measure of the guilt.

There is, however, much inquiry about one saying that Christ spoke. He said, "Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to men who repent, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven."

"Though someone speaks a slanderous word against me, it will be forgiven him if he does penance. But truly, whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this world or in the world to come."
There is no forgiveness of sins except through the Holy Spirit. There is one Almighty Father, who begot one Son from himself.
The Father is not held in common as Father by the Son and the Holy Spirit, because he is not the son of them both.
The Holy Spirit is truly shared in common by the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of them both, that is, the Love and Will of them both, through whom sins are forgiven.
Truly, the work of the Holy Trinity is always indivisible; nevertheless, all forgiveness belongs to the Holy Spirit, just as the birth belongs to Christ alone.
They cannot be named all together at once, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, but they are never separated from one another anywhere for any space of time.
In all works they are together, although it belongs particularly to the Father that he begot a Son, and to the Son belongs the birth, and to the Holy Spirit the procession.

The Son is the Father's Wisdom, eternally begotten of the Father; the Holy Spirit is not begotten, because he is not a son, but he is the Love and Will of them both, eternally proceeding from them both,
through whom we have forgiveness of sins, just as we have redemption through Christ; and nevertheless, in each work the Holy Trinity is working indivisibly.
He speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit who, with an unrepentant heart, persists in wicked deeds and scorns the forgiveness that rests on the gift of the Holy Spirit:
then his guilt will be beyond redemption, because he himself shuts off from himself the way of forgiveness by his hard-heartedness.
To those who repent it will be forgiven, to those who scorn it, never. Let us pray to the Almighty Father, who made us through his Wisdom and gave us life through his Holy Spirit,
that through that same Spirit he may grant us forgiveness of our sins, just as he redeemed us from the devil's bondage through his one only-begotten Son.

Praise and glory be to the eternal Father, who never had a beginning, and to his only Son, who is eternally from him, and to the Holy Spirit, who is eternally from them both, the three one Almighty God, indivisible, reigning forever in eternity. Amen.
